--- title: "Implementing the BARTverse" author: - name: "[Ajinkya Kokandakar](https://ajinkya-k.github.io)" email: ajinkya@stat.wisc.edu orcid: 0000-0001-6628-2272 affiliations: - name: 'ajinkya-k.github.io' city: Madison state: WI url: https://ajinkya-k.github.io department: Statistics date: "2025-02-26" format: revealjs: slide-number: true smaller: true progress: true --- ## Follow-up: Forcing a split on a variable 1. If the variable is binary, use BCF: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}(Y | X = x, Z = z) &= f(x) + z \cdot g(x) \\ &= \begin{cases} f(x) && \text{if } z = 0 \\ f(x) + g(x) && \text{if } z = 1 \end{cases} , \end{align} so the "treatment effect" is $g(x)$
2. If we have a continuous variable, - initialize the trees to be split on that variable - Use initialized trees in the MCMC The `flexBART` package, _can_ start at any arbitrarily initialized trees. ## Work in progress - Use a Laplace approximation when updating trees. - This is useful beacause we can use a single formulation for any expoential family - This also means we can reuse _a lot_ of the code - For any model $y ~ f(x; \theta)$ we simply need: 1. first log-derivative w.r.t parameters, i.e. the score function $\displaystyle \frac{\partial \log f}{\partial \theta}$ 2. second log-derivative w.r.t parameters, i.e. $\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2 \log f}{\partial \theta^2}$ ## Exploiting the generality We can reuse a lot of code by using an abstract class in `C++` ```{cpp} class Model { public: virtual double score(double y, double θ) = 0; virtual double jacobian(double y, double θ) = 0; double draw_proposal(double y); } ``` For each specific distribution say Poisson implement the score and jacobian functions: ```{c++} class Poisson: Model { public: virtual double score(double y, double θ) { return (y / θ - 1) }; virtual double jacobian(double y, double θ) { 1 / θ }; } ```
